questions.questionText: How many moles are present in 9.0 g of water, H₂O, when its molar mass is 18.0 g mol⁻¹?
questions.explanation: Amount in moles equals mass divided by molar mass, so 9.0 ÷ 18.0 = 0.50 mol.

curriculum.objective: Calculate amounts of substance and interpret atomic or mass-spectrometric data using appropriate chemical relationships.

questions.questionText: A gas occupies 600 cm³ at constant temperature and 100 kPa. What volume will it occupy at 150 kPa?
questions.explanation: Boyle’s law gives p₁V₁ = p₂V₂, so V₂ = 100 × 600 ÷ 150 = 400 cm³.

curriculum.objective: Calculate amounts of substance and interpret atomic or mass-spectrometric data using appropriate chemical relationships.

questions.questionText: Chlorine has isotopes ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl. A sample contains 75% ³⁵Cl. What is its relative atomic mass?
questions.explanation: The weighted mean is (0.75 × 35) + (0.25 × 37), which equals 35.5.

curriculum.objective: Calculate amounts of substance and interpret atomic or mass-spectrometric data using appropriate chemical relationships.

questions.questionText: A hydrocarbon contains 85.7% carbon and 14.3% hydrogen by mass. Which empirical formula is consistent with these data?
questions.explanation: For 100 g, carbon gives 85.7 ÷ 12 ≈ 7.14 mol and hydrogen gives 14.3 mol, a 1:2 ratio.

curriculum.subskill: Convert mass composition to mole ratio
curriculum.objective: Calculate amounts of substance and interpret atomic or mass-spectrometric data using appropriate chemical relationships.

questions.questionText: Which type of bonding involves electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions?
questions.explanation: Ionic bonding is the strong electrostatic attraction between positive and negative ions in a lattice.

curriculum.objective: Explain and predict properties of substances from bonding, intermolecular forces and three-dimensional structure.

questions.questionText: Why does magnesium have a higher melting point than sodium?
options: Magnesium supplies more delocalised electrons and forms more highly charged ions
questions.correctAnswer: Magnesium supplies more delocalised electrons and forms more highly charged ions
questions.explanation: Mg²⁺ ions and two delocalised electrons per atom create stronger metallic attraction than Na⁺ ions with one electron.

curriculum.objective: Explain and predict properties of substances from bonding, intermolecular forces and three-dimensional structure.

questions.questionText: Which molecule is non-polar even though each of its bonds is polar?
questions.explanation: CO₂ is linear, so its two equal C=O bond dipoles act in opposite directions and cancel.

curriculum.objective: Explain and predict properties of substances from bonding, intermolecular forces and three-dimensional structure.

questions.questionText: Which change best explains why graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not?
options: Graphite contains mobile ions between its layers
Diamond has weaker covalent bonds than graphite
Graphite molecules transfer electrons by collision
Each carbon in graphite contributes one electron to a delocalised system
questions.correctAnswer: Each carbon in graphite contributes one electron to a delocalised system
questions.explanation: Three bonds per carbon in graphite leave one electron delocalised across a layer, while all four valence electrons are localised in diamond.

curriculum.objective: Explain and predict properties of substances from bonding, intermolecular forces and three-dimensional structure.

questions.questionText: What is the sign of ΔH for an exothermic reaction?
options: It must equal the activation energy
questions.explanation: An exothermic reaction releases energy to the surroundings, so the products have lower enthalpy and ΔH is negative.

curriculum.objective: Apply energetic, kinetic and equilibrium principles to explain observations and predict the effect of changing conditions.

questions.questionText: A catalyst increases the rate of a reversible reaction. What happens to the equilibrium constant at the same temperature?
questions.explanation: A catalyst lowers activation energies in both directions equally; it speeds equilibration but does not change K at fixed temperature.

curriculum.objective: Apply energetic, kinetic and equilibrium principles to explain observations and predict the effect of changing conditions.

questions.questionText: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), which change shifts equilibrium toward ammonia?
questions.explanation: Higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules, so equilibrium shifts from four gas moles toward two moles of ammonia.

curriculum.objective: Apply energetic, kinetic and equilibrium principles to explain observations and predict the effect of changing conditions.

questions.questionText: A reaction has ΔH = +40 kJ mol⁻¹ and activation energy 75 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the activation energy of the reverse reaction?
questions.explanation: For an endothermic forward reaction, products lie 40 kJ mol⁻¹ higher; the reverse barrier is 75 − 40 = 35 kJ mol⁻¹.

curriculum.objective: Apply energetic, kinetic and equilibrium principles to explain observations and predict the effect of changing conditions.

questions.questionText: What is the oxidation number of sulfur in SO₄²⁻?
questions.explanation: Four oxygens contribute −8 overall; sulfur must be +6 so that the ion has a total charge of −2.

curriculum.objective: Determine oxidation changes and use periodic or inorganic trends to interpret reactions and properties.

questions.questionText: Which species is oxidised in Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s)?
questions.explanation: Zinc loses two electrons and its oxidation number rises from 0 to +2, so zinc is oxidised.

curriculum.objective: Determine oxidation changes and use periodic or inorganic trends to interpret reactions and properties.

questions.questionText: Why does atomic radius generally decrease across Period 3 from sodium to chlorine?
options: The number of occupied shells decreases
Nuclear charge increases while added electrons enter the same main shell
The atoms lose all valence electrons
questions.correctAnswer: Nuclear charge increases while added electrons enter the same main shell
questions.explanation: Increasing proton number strengthens attraction to electrons in the same shell, while shielding changes comparatively little.

curriculum.objective: Determine oxidation changes and use periodic or inorganic trends to interpret reactions and properties.

questions.questionText: In acidic solution, MnO₄⁻ is reduced to Mn²⁺. How many electrons are gained by each manganese atom?
questions.explanation: Manganese changes from +7 in permanganate to +2 in Mn²⁺, a decrease of five oxidation-number units and a gain of five electrons.

curriculum.objective: Determine oxidation changes and use periodic or inorganic trends to interpret reactions and properties.

questions.questionText: Which functional group is present in ethanol?
questions.explanation: Ethanol is an alcohol and contains the hydroxyl functional group, represented by –OH.

curriculum.objective: Identify organic structures and use reaction evidence or analytical data to predict products and distinguish compounds.

questions.questionText: What is the major product when ethene reacts with steam in the presence of an acid catalyst?
questions.explanation: Hydration adds H and OH across the carbon-carbon double bond of ethene to form ethanol.

curriculum.objective: Identify organic structures and use reaction evidence or analytical data to predict products and distinguish compounds.

questions.questionText: Which observation distinguishes an aldehyde from a ketone using Tollens’ reagent?
options: The aldehyde produces a silver mirror
questions.correctAnswer: The aldehyde produces a silver mirror
questions.explanation: An aldehyde reduces Tollens’ reagent to metallic silver, while an ordinary ketone does not react under these conditions.

curriculum.objective: Identify organic structures and use reaction evidence or analytical data to predict products and distinguish compounds.

questions.questionText: A compound with formula C₃H₆O gives an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH but no silver mirror with Tollens’ reagent. Which structure fits the evidence?
questions.explanation: The 2,4-DNPH result confirms a carbonyl group, while the negative Tollens’ test identifies the compound as the ketone propanone.

curriculum.objective: Identify organic structures and use reaction evidence or analytical data to predict products and distinguish compounds.
